title: The Value of the Cloud, Shared Responsibility, and Availability
objective: Explain the benefits of the cloud and the responsibilities of AWS and the customer for each service. Explain the difference between Regions and Availability Zones using deployment examples.

sections.title: Use the Amount You Need, When You Need It
paragraphs: The value of the cloud lies not in owning servers, but in being able to use the computing resources you need for only as long as you need them. For example, when a sales department must handle an increase in order processing only at the end of the month, operations staff consider a mechanism that can scale capacity up or down according to actual demand rather than maintaining the same number of servers at all times for the forecast peak load.

Elasticity is the ability to add resources when demand increases and reduce them when demand falls. Amazon EC2 provides computing capacity, but mechanisms such as Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling must be combined with it to automatically increase or decrease the number of instances according to demand. Because scaling itself does not guarantee availability, users must first decide which failures they need to prepare for and how much interruption they can tolerate.

The AWS Well-Architected Framework provides a framework for considering design trade-offs through its six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, and sustainability. Rather than memorizing the names of specific services, it is important to develop the ability to make decisions based on business conditions and quality priorities.

sources.label: The Six Pillars of the Well-Architected Framework

sections.title: Responsibilities vary by service type
paragraphs: Under the shared responsibility model, AWS protects the cloud itself, including data centers, physical hardware, and the underlying network. Customers, in turn, protect the data, identities, access permissions, and service configurations they place in the cloud. It is not a model in which either party handles everything alone.

For Amazon EC2, AWS manages the physical hosts. Customers update the guest OS and manage access to application configurations and data. For Amazon S3, AWS manages the server operating system. Customers are responsible for classifying the data they store, managing access permissions for buckets, and configuring encryption.

When adopting a new service, first separate the layers managed by AWS, the layers configured by the customer, and who verifies the results of those configurations. This organization helps avoid the misconception that choosing a managed service eliminates the need for security measures.

sections.title: Designing Deployments Around Failure Scope
paragraphs: An AWS Region is a geographic location, and each Region contains multiple Availability Zones. An Availability Zone consists of one or more independent data centers with redundant power and networking. A Region and an Availability Zone are not the same unit.

For example, if the person responsible for an online ordering service wants to reduce downtime caused by a failure affecting one Availability Zone, they may consider using multiple Availability Zones in the same Region. This does not mean preventing every failure; it is a decision to improve availability for the anticipated scope of failure.

When selecting a service, first confirm the users, the data involved, the acceptable downtime, and any legal or contractual constraints, then consider where to deploy it. The decision should include not only placing resources in multiple locations, but also recovery methods, data handling, and operational procedures.

sections.title: Compare migration and costs based on the prerequisites
paragraphs: When migrating to the cloud, organizations choose a strategy by confirming what will be migrated, business priorities, the amount of downtime they can tolerate, and existing licenses. AWS CAF is a framework for advancing cloud adoption from the perspectives of business, people, governance, platform, security, and operations. Migration is not merely the task of moving services; it is an initiative to create an environment that the organization can operate.

Cloud economics distinguishes fixed costs for purchasing infrastructure in advance from variable costs that change with actual usage. Rightsizing, automation, and economies of scale help inform decisions that reduce unnecessary idle resources and manual work. When moving existing software, organizations compare bring-your-own-license and license-included options, taking contract terms and operational burden into account.

If reducing costs is the sole objective, necessary reliability or security may be compromised. Users make decisions by considering the value of the workload alongside the six pillars and explicitly identifying which constraints should take priority.

sources.label: CLF-C02 Domain 1: Migration and Cloud Economics

checkpoints.prompt: A retail company's operations staff manages an order application running on Amazon EC2. During a monthly security review, which task is the customer's responsibility?

choices.text: Replace failed components in the physical servers that run EC2.
choices.explanation: Managing the physical servers and data center facilities is AWS's responsibility to protect the cloud itself.

choices.text: Apply the required updates to the EC2 guest operating system.
choices.explanation: For EC2, AWS manages the physical infrastructure, while the customer manages the guest operating system and the settings on it.
The underlying network equipment is part of the cloud infrastructure managed by AWS.

choices.text: Manage physical access to and from AWS data centers.
choices.explanation: Physical protection of the data centers is AWS's responsibility.

checkpoints.prompt: The service owner of a video streaming company wants to reduce the risk that order acceptance will stop because of a failure affecting a single Availability Zone. Which deployment should be considered first within the same Region?

choices.text: Deploy two identical configurations within the same Availability Zone.
choices.explanation: Limiting deployment to the same Availability Zone does not prepare for a failure affecting that Zone.

choices.text: Use multiple Availability Zones within the same Region.
choices.explanation: Because Availability Zones consist of independent groups of data centers, using multiple Zones is the first choice for separating the expected failure scope within the same Region.

choices.text: Only increase the size of a single EC2 instance.
choices.explanation: Increasing capacity does not change the failure scope caused by dependence on a single deployment location.

choices.text: Replicate all data to a local laptop.
choices.explanation: This approach is not an AWS availability design and is not appropriate as a deployment decision for service continuity.

checkpoints.prompt: The person responsible for a business unit running an advertising campaign wants to handle traffic that is low during normal periods but surges immediately after an announcement. Which best describes the value of increasing or decreasing computing resources based on demand?

choices.text: Keeping the same number of servers throughout the year to prepare for peak traffic.
choices.explanation: Maintaining fixed capacity at all times does not describe elasticity, which involves adjusting capacity to match demand.

choices.text: Increasing capacity to match demand for the required period and reducing it when demand decreases.
choices.explanation: The essence of elasticity is the ability to increase or decrease resources as demand changes. To automatically adjust the number of EC2 instances, combine it with services such as Auto Scaling.

choices.text: Preventing all failures with a single service.
choices.explanation: Elasticity is a property related to increasing or decreasing capacity; it does not mean preventing all failures.

choices.text: Allowing users to avoid configuring access permissions.
choices.explanation: Configuring access permissions is the user's responsibility under the shared responsibility model and is a separate concept from elasticity.
